newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Cardenas launches political comeback.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Cardenas launches political comeback.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Mexicans gathered in Mexico City's central square on Friday to help launch a campaign by left-wing veteran Cuauhtemoc Cardenas to become this capital city's first elected mayor.

Chants of "Viva Cuauhtemoc" rose from the crowd of about 30,000 supporters of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) that assembled in front of the national palace and city hall despite rain and a long holiday weekend.

Polls show Cardenas, son of a popular ex-president, as the front runner for what is arguably the country's second most powerful post and the most widely-watched political contest of the July mid-term elections.

After nearly winning the 1988 presidential race, but faltering badly in a second try three years ago, Cardenas' bid to become mayor of this city of more than 16 million people has breathed new life into a political career considered moribund just a few months ago.
"The other parties all view us as the victors. But we must not get complacent and rest on our laurels before the race is won," the 62-year old politician said.

A recent poll by Indermerc/Louis Harris put Cardenas nine percentage points ahead of his nearest rival, conservative Carlos Castillo Peraza. The candidate for the ruling Instutitional Revolutionary Party (PRI) was in third place.

The leftist candidate repeatedly blasted the PRI, which has held power for 68 years, as a haven for corruption following a series of political scandals in the past few years that have eroded government support.

"Enough of corruption ... we want a city transparent in both its air and administration," Cardenas told residents of this polluted metropolis, which will elect its mayor for the first time rather than have the post hand-picked by the president.

He also blamed the government's economic policies for the 1994-1995 economic crisis, the country's worst recession since the Great Depression -- offering instead a vision of economic prosperity and social justice.

Supporters, mostly lower middle-class professionals and the poor, waved yellow and black flags of the PRD party and chanted anti-government slogans, blaming it for a widening gap between the haves and have-nots that has made Cardenas' message increasingly relevant -- even to the middle class.
"Cardenas will win because he is honest and he cares about the people," Hector Miguel Barrera, a 68-year-old major in the Mexican army who attended the rally said.

Cardenas enjoys widespread sympathy among Mexicans in part because of his father Lazaro's hugely popular 1934-1940 administration. Many believe electoral fraud cheated the younger Cardenas out of a presidential win in 1988.
Reflecting voter fears the PRI could use dirty tricks to keep Mexico City, Cardenas vowed he would not tolerate fraud.
"This time around, we will not just have the force of reason on our side, but the capacity to be able to back it up," Cardenas said, prompting shouts of "duro, duro" or "tough, tough" from the crowd.

Most observers expect Cardenas' lead to narrow as his lesser known opponents campaign in earnest. Castillo Peraza's National Action Party (PAN) is widely viewed as the strongest opposition party but was hurt when its charismatic lawyer Diego Fernandez chose not to run.
